[1] (Guide to Banana Bunchy Top Disease: Surveillance, control, and product, p.9) Introduction Banana Bunchy Top Disease (BBTD), caused by the Banana Bunchy Top Virus (BBTV) (formal species name: Babuvirus musae), is one of the most serious threats to banana and plantain cultivation in Africa. The disease severely reduces fruit production, affecting food security and the livelihoods of millions of people. In sub-Saharan Africa, where over 70 million people depend on bananas and plantains for food and income, the spread of BBTD poses an urgent challenge. Because the virus is a rapidly spreading invasive species, BBTD often becomes established in communities where awareness of its symptoms and management strategies is limited. In heavily affected areas, yield losses can surpass 90%, often gradually leading to production collapse at the farm/landscape/ regional scale. The disease not only threatens smallholder farming systems but also undermines national seed systems and the
[2] (Guide to Banana Bunchy Top Disease: Surveillance, control, and product, p.23) Figure 16. Distribution of Banana Bunchy Top Disease (BBTD) in Africa. To date, BBTD has been reported in 18 countries across the continent, highlighted in orange on the map. Understanding the distribution of BBTD is critical for disease monitoring and management efforts across Africa. Figure created with MapChart.net.19 19 MapChart. [Online map creation tool]. https://www.mapchart.net/ 3.2 How Banana Bunchy Top Virus is spread BBTV is spread through two main ways: 1. Banana aphid. The banana aphid (Pentalonia nigronervosa) acquires BBTV by feeding on the sap of an infected banana plant. When it moves to a healthy plant and feeds again, it transmits the virus, thereby spreading the disease. This aphid-mediated transmission is responsible for local spread of BBTV within a farm or between nearby farms. Infected planting materials. BBTV can spread locally and over longer distances, including across national borders, through the movement of infected planting materials such as suckers that are transported and planted in new areas. Therefore, controlling banana aphid dispersal and ensuring that planting materials are virusfree are essential strategies for controlling BBTD.
[3] (Guide to Banana Bunchy Top Disease: Surveillance, control, and product, p.30) Figure 23. Early symptoms of BBTD. Left: Midrib and leaf lamina with dark green dots and streaks (the Morse-code symptom). Right: Close-up of a banana leaf showing distinctive Morse code-symptoms along the veins of the leaf lamina, and also J-hook markings where the dark streaks bend down to meet the midrib. The midrib also has dark streaks. Photos: A.B. Omondi, Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT. The leaves start to develop chlorotic (yellowing) and necrotic margins (edges), but the leaves are of normal size (Fig. 24). As the disease progresses, the bunchy top symptoms become obvious. New leaves that emerge become progressively shorter and narrower. The leaves appear brittle with wavy, chlorotic (yellow) and necrotic (dying) edges. Eventually, the leaves stop Figure 24. Intermediate BBTD symptoms. Chlorosis and onset of necrosis of the leaf margin. Photo: A.B. Omondi, Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT.

[1] (Post harvest management guide for common beans: A guide for farmers an, p.29) Bagging and packaging Once grain is sufficiently dry and cleaned it should be put in storage. Grain may be stored on farm for different length of time as follows: ▌ Short term (e.g. <3 months)- before it is moved to the next link in the market chain e.g collection point of the Farmer Organization or Cereal Board or School Medium to long term (3-12 months)- where farmers keep grain for household consumption of for sale at a time when the process are more favorable There are many options available to farmers for storing their grain and protect it against pest attack. Storage types for safe storage of grain by smallholder households Storage type If used >6 months, grain quality declines than in tother store types Very heavy so can not be moved to new location Takes up fixed space in the house whether full or empty Extra sealing needed to make it hermitic, then no access for 2 weeks
[2] (Post harvest management guide for common beans: A guide for farmers an, p.13) Keep the store absolutely clean. Remove any spilt grain immediately as it attracts rodents. Store bags in tidy stacks set up on pallets, ensuring that there is a space of 1 meter all round the stack Store any empty or old bags and fumigation sheets on pallets, and if possible in separate stores! Keep the store free of rubbish in order not to provide the animals with any places to hide or nest! Keep the area surrounding the store free of tall weeds so as not to give the animals any cover! They have an aversion to crossing open spaces. Keep the area in the vicinity of the store free of any stagnant water and ensure that rainwater is drained away, as it can be used as source of drinking water. Cats can help eliminate the rodents from the stores In extreme infestation, use rodenticides to eliminate the pests
[3] (Post harvest management guide for common beans: A guide for farmers an, p.13) b. Rodents Rats have been estimated to damage more than 1% of the world cereal crops and, in developing countries, estimates of 3–5% have commonly been reported. In beans, rodents mainly cause damage to storage facilities, bags and also cause contamination of the grain. There are around 50 diseases which can be transferred to humans by rodents, including typhoid, paratyphoid, and scabies. Damage caused by rodents Rats and mice cause losses in a number of ways: — Feeding on stored produce: Rats consume about 25 gm of food per day and mice eat approximately 3–4 gm per day. Besides eating stored produce, rodents contaminate a lot of the stored produce with urine, faeces, hair and pathogenic agents. Contaminated grain is often declared unfit for human consumption. Damage to material and equipment: Rodents damage tarpaulins, bags, pallets, sprayers and to the store itself (cables, doors) and equipment e.g. scales and store records. Management of rodents Good store management and preventive measures taken as part of an integrated control program can help to deal with these factors. —
How do I keep rats out of my grain store?
Keep the area surrounding the store free of tall weeds so as not to give the animals any cover. [2] Remove any spilt grain immediately as it attracts rodents. [2]
